title: PAUL REMEMBERED THEIR NAMES. WHY HAS THE CHURCH ALMOST FORGOTTEN THEM?
paragraphs: PAUL REMEMBERED THEIR NAMES. WHY HAS THE CHURCH ALMOST FORGOTTEN THEM?

They worked hard for the Gospel. They served when following Jesus could cost them everything. And nearly 2,000 years later, their names are still written in Scripture. What Paul said about these women in Romans 16 may challenge the way we recognize faithfulness, honor sacrifice, and understand who truly matters in the Kingdom of God.
There is something heartbreaking about being faithful and feeling forgotten.
You show up. You serve. You sacrifice. You pray when everyone else is sleeping. You give what you can, even when nobody knows what it costs you.
And sometimes, the people who benefit most from your faithfulness never even remember your name.
But imagine something.
Imagine the apostle Paul, writing a letter that would eventually become part of the Holy Scriptures, suddenly stopping to mention you.
Not because you were famous.
Not because you commanded an army, preached before thousands, or possessed an impressive religious title.
But because you worked hard for Jesus.
And your faithfulness mattered enough to be remembered.
That is exactly what happened to several women in the sixteenth chapter of Romans.
And here is the question that should make us uncomfortable:
If the Holy Spirit preserved their names in Scripture, why do so many Christians barely know who they were?
We know Paul.
We know Peter.
We know Timothy.
But how many believers have heard a sermon about Mary of Romans 16?
How many know Tryphena?
Tryphosa?
Persis?
These were not imaginary characters added to make a biblical story more interesting.
They were real women.
Real disciples.
Real servants of Jesus Christ.
And Paul wanted the church in Rome to remember them.
Listen to his words.
“Greet Mary, who bestowed much labour on us.” — Romans 16:6, KJV
“Salute Tryphena and Tryphosa, who labour in the Lord. Salute the beloved Persis, which laboured much in the Lord.” — Romans 16:12, KJV
Read those verses again.
Slowly.
Paul did not describe these women as decorations around the important people.
He remembered their labor.
He recognized their contribution.
He publicly honored their devotion to the Lord.
And hidden inside the original Greek is something even more beautiful.
In Romans 16:6, Paul uses the word ἐκοπίασεν (ekopiasen), from the verb κοπιάω (kopiaō).
It means to labor, toil, or work hard, often with the sense of weariness and exertion.
This was not casual participation.
This was costly effort.
The kind of work that leaves a person tired.
The kind of service that requires perseverance.
The kind of faithfulness that may never receive applause.
Paul says Mary labored much.
In Romans 16:12, Tryphena and Tryphosa are described with κοπιώσας (kopiōsas), a participle referring to women laboring in the Lord.
And Persis?
Paul uses the same verb family again: ἐκοπίασεν (ekopiasen).
She had worked hard in the Lord.
There is a beautiful consistency here.
Paul did not merely remember their names.
He remembered what their devotion had cost them.
And perhaps that is where this passage begins to reach into our own lives.
Because somebody reading this knows what it means to keep serving while feeling invisible.
Maybe you are the mother who has spent years praying for a child who no longer wants anything to do with God.
Maybe you are the woman who cleans the church after everyone else has gone home.
Maybe you are the sister who quietly helps struggling families but never tells anyone what she has given.
Maybe you have spent years teaching children the Scriptures, visiting the sick, encouraging exhausted believers, or carrying burdens that never appear in a church announcement.
Maybe you have wondered whether your life matters because your ministry does not have a microphone.
And perhaps you have whispered something you would never say publicly.
“Lord, does anybody even see what I do?”
Romans 16 does not promise that every act of service will receive public recognition.
But it reminds us that the Kingdom of God has never been built only through the people standing in front of crowds.
And Scripture gives us an even greater assurance.
“For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name.” — Hebrews 6:10, KJV
God does not forget faithful love.
Not the prayer.
Not the sacrifice.
Not the obedience.
Not the quiet act of mercy offered in the name of Jesus.
Even when people overlook it.
But there is another detail in Romans 16 that deserves our attention.
Paul did not simply say these women were hardworking.
He located their labor in relation to Christ.
They labored in the Lord.
That changes everything.
Because the value of Christian service is not measured merely by how exhausted we become, how many activities we attend, or how much responsibility we carry.
A person can be busy with religious activities and still lose sight of Jesus.
A person can serve publicly while privately craving recognition.
A person can work tirelessly and forget the One for whom the work was supposed to be done.
These women were commended because their labor belonged to the Lord.
And that distinction matters.
The Gospel is not a competition to see who can do the most for God. It is the good news that Jesus Christ has done what sinners could never do for themselves.
We are not saved because we work hard enough.
We are saved by grace through faith in Christ.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
And then Paul immediately tells us that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Do you see the order?
Grace comes first.
Good works follow.
We do not labor to purchase God's acceptance.
We labor because, through Christ, we have received mercy we could never earn.
That is what makes the faithful service of these women so beautiful.
Their names were not preserved as evidence that human effort can save the soul.
Their names testify that the grace of Jesus Christ produces lives of meaningful service.
And this was not the only place where Paul recognized women who served the Gospel.
At the beginning of Romans 16, he commends Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, and asks the Roman believers to receive her and assist her.
Paul describes her using the Greek word διάκονον (diakonon), the accusative form of diakonos, meaning servant or minister, a term also used in contexts of recognized Christian ministry.
He also calls her a προστάτις (prostatis), a word commonly understood as a patron, benefactor, or protector.
The precise implications of these descriptions for later church offices are debated among Christians.
But the text itself is clear about something that should not be controversial.
Phoebe served the church.
She supported many people, including Paul.
And Paul publicly commended her.
Then he greets Prisca, also known as Priscilla, and Aquila.
He calls them his fellow workers in Christ Jesus.
He says they risked their own necks for his life.
And he acknowledges that the Gentile churches had reason to be thankful for them.
Think about that.
A husband and wife serving together.
Risking themselves.
Helping advance the Gospel.
And Paul refuses to let their sacrifice disappear into silence.
Romans 16 also includes Junia, whom Paul mentions alongside Andronicus as his fellow prisoners and as people who were in Christ before him.
The Greek description of their relationship to the apostles has been interpreted differently, and Christians debate the precise significance of that wording.
But there is no need to exaggerate the passage to appreciate its testimony.
Paul remembered these believers.
He honored their suffering.
He recognized their place in the story of the early church.
And that should teach us something about how carefully we ought to read the Bible.
We do not need to force Scripture to answer every modern controversy before allowing it to speak.
Nor should we erase what it plainly says because its testimony challenges our assumptions.
The text honors women who worked hard in the Lord.
That fact deserves to be preached, taught, remembered, and celebrated.
And yet, something else is worth considering.
We know these women's names.
But we know relatively little about their personal lives.
Scripture does not tell us whether Mary ever felt discouraged.
It does not tell us what Tryphena and Tryphosa sacrificed.
It does not explain every difficulty Persis endured.
We must not invent their biographies.
But we can recognize the humanity behind their names.
They lived in a world where following Christ could involve social rejection, economic hardship, and, in some circumstances, persecution.
Their labor was not performed in a comfortable modern environment with all the conveniences we take for granted.
They belonged to real communities with real needs.
And in those communities, they worked.
They persevered.
They served the Lord.
And here is the part that makes me wonder about us.
What if some of the people we barely notice today are among the most faithful servants in our churches?
What if the person whose name never appears on the ministry poster has spent more time praying for broken families than the person standing on the platform?
What if the woman who quietly visits a lonely widow is demonstrating the love of Christ more clearly than someone whose ministry receives thousands of online reactions?
What if the believer who patiently disciples one struggling person for years is doing work that will bear fruit long after today's applause has disappeared?
We cannot see the full measure of another person's faithfulness.
Only God can.
That is why we should be careful about confusing visibility with spiritual significance.
Jesus Himself warned against practicing righteousness merely to be seen by others (Matthew 6:1).
And He taught that even a cup of cold water given to one of His little ones because that person belongs to Him would not go unrewarded (Matthew 10:42).
The Kingdom of God has a way of overturning our assumptions about greatness.
And nowhere is that reversal clearer than at the cross.
Because the center of Christianity is not a successful religious personality.
It is a crucified and risen Savior.
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, entered our broken world.
He welcomed the rejected.
He showed compassion to the suffering.
He called sinners to repentance.
He exposed religious hypocrisy.
He honored humble faith.
He bore our sins on the cross.
And He rose again, conquering death.
The One who deserved all glory willingly humbled Himself for our salvation.
Philippians 2:8 tells us that He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
So how can we claim to follow a humble Savior while treating humble service as insignificant?
How can we celebrate the Gospel of grace while withholding honor from those who quietly serve its mission?
How can we read Romans 16 and fail to notice that Paul took time to remember people whose labor mattered?
And perhaps the most searching question is not why their names are rarely mentioned.
Perhaps it is this:
Have we become so impressed by public platforms that we have forgotten how to recognize Christlike faithfulness?
That question is not only for church leaders.
It is for all of us.
For the person who wants recognition.
For the person who feels overlooked.
For the person who assumes that a ministry must be large to be valuable.
For the person who has quietly resented someone else's opportunity.
For the person who has stopped serving because nobody said thank you.
And for the person who has forgotten to thank the faithful believers God has placed nearby.
Maybe Romans 16 is inviting us to repent.
Not necessarily of some dramatic public scandal.
Sometimes repentance begins with something painfully ordinary.
Pride.
Envy.
Indifference.
The hunger for applause.
The habit of overlooking people.
The belief that our service only matters when somebody notices.
But Jesus does not expose our hearts merely to leave us ashamed.
He calls us to turn back to Him.
He offers forgiveness.
He restores what sin has damaged.
He teaches us to love differently.
And through His grace, He transforms people who once lived for themselves into servants who live for His glory.
That is the beautiful movement from scandal to grace.
Not the denial of our failures.
Not the pretending that the church has always honored everyone perfectly.
Not the rewriting of biblical history to satisfy our preferences.
But the confession that we need the mercy of Christ, and that His mercy can change how we see, honor, and serve one another.
And if you are one of those believers who feels forgotten, there is something I want you to remember tonight.
Your worth is not established by how much you accomplish.
It is not established by whether your church recognizes you.
It is not established by your ministry title, social media following, or the number of people who thank you.
Your worth is not something you have to earn through exhaustion.
The love of God in Christ is not a salary paid to the hardest worker.
It is grace.
So serve faithfully.
But do not destroy yourself trying to prove you matter.
Rest when you need to rest.
Ask for help when the burden is too heavy.
Let other believers carry responsibilities alongside you.
Even Jesus told His disciples to come away and rest for a while (Mark 6:31).
Faithfulness is not the same as endless exhaustion.
And when you are tempted to believe that your quiet obedience is meaningless, remember Mary.
Remember Tryphena.
Remember Tryphosa.
Remember Persis.
Women whose names remain in the Word of God because Paul, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, recorded his greetings and recognized their labor.
We do not know everything they did.
But we know enough to say that their service was worth honoring.
And maybe we should begin doing the same.
Thank the woman who has prayed for your family.
Encourage the believer who has faithfully taught the Scriptures for years.
Recognize the people who serve without demanding attention.
Tell your children about the faithful women of the Bible, not only the most familiar names.
Read Romans 16 with your family.
Let your church hear those names again.
Not to elevate human beings above Jesus Christ.
But to honor the grace of God at work in His people.
Because every faithful servant ultimately points beyond themselves to the Lord who saved them.
And there is one more thing I do not want you to miss.
Paul's greetings were personal.
He knew names.
He remembered relationships.
He acknowledged sacrifice.
His theology did not prevent him from loving actual people.
It taught him to love them more deeply.
That is something our generation desperately needs.
We can publish Bible verses every day and still fail to notice the hurting person beside us.
We can debate ministry roles and forget to encourage the people already serving.
We can talk about revival while neglecting the ordinary obedience through which God strengthens His church.
But genuine discipleship is not merely knowing the right arguments.
It is becoming more like Jesus.
It is learning to speak truth with love.
It is remembering that every believer belongs to a body in which the members need one another (1 Corinthians 12).
It is refusing to treat another person's faithful service as disposable.
And it is recognizing that the Gospel is powerful enough to transform not only our eternal destiny, but also our everyday relationships.
So I want to ask you something personal.
Who is your Mary?
Who is your Tryphena?
Who is your Tryphosa?
Who is your Persis?
Who has labored faithfully in your life without receiving the gratitude they deserve?
Maybe it is your mother.
Maybe it is a sister in Christ.
Maybe it is an elderly believer who has been praying for you for decades.
Maybe it is a teacher, a mentor, a missionary, a volunteer, or a friend.
And maybe today is the day you stop assuming they already know how grateful you are.
Tell them.
While you still can.
Because encouragement given today is far more meaningful than praise offered only when someone is gone.
And if you are the one who has been serving quietly, perhaps your heart needs a different reminder.
You do not have to become famous to be faithful.
You do not have to be publicly recognized to be loved by God.
You do not have to turn your life into a performance to make it count.
Remain in Christ.
Receive His grace.
Walk in obedience.
Love His people.
And leave the final accounting of your labor to Him.
The same Lord who sees the sparrow fall knows the lives of His children.
And the Savior who gave Himself for you is worthy of your trust even when people fail to notice your sacrifice.
If this article brought someone to mind, please do not let the moment pass.
And if you are comfortable sharing, comment the name of a woman who has helped you follow Christ, and tell us what God taught you through her.
Perhaps she will read your words.
Perhaps someone else will be encouraged by her testimony.
Perhaps a younger believer will discover that a life devoted to Jesus is worth far more than public applause.
If you are the one who has been quietly struggling, you can simply comment, “Lord, help me remain faithful.”
You do not have to explain your whole story to strangers.
God already knows it.
The early church was strengthened through believers who worked together for the Gospel.
We still need that kind of faithfulness today.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality around a platform.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell the grace of God.
But to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture-centered teaching, biblical encouragement, repentance, healing, and discipleship.
There is room here for people who want to grow.
For people who are learning.
For people who have fallen and need to repent.
For people who are exhausted.
For people who need to hear again that salvation is found in Jesus Christ, not in religious performance.
But I want to be clear about something because biblical truth matters more than fundraising.
Christians can glorify God through faithful obedience, generosity, prayer, service, and many other expressions of love for Him.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing rather than pressured.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
And the Bible also teaches the importance of supporting faithful Gospel ministry (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
You may regard it as part of your personal giving to Gospel ministry, while continuing to prayerfully honor your responsibilities and commitments to your local church.
The free resources remain an important part of the mission because biblical nourishment should not be treated as something available only to those who can pay.
Because the mission is bigger than any one page.
The mission is the Gospel.
The message is Jesus.
And the hope is that more people will come to know Him, repent of sin, trust in His finished work, and grow as His disciples.
One day, our names may be forgotten by history.
Our photographs may fade.
Our social media pages may disappear.
Our achievements may become footnotes in somebody else's story.
But the grace of God in Jesus Christ is not temporary.
And the eternal life He gives to those who belong to Him cannot be taken away.
Paul remembered Mary.
He remembered Tryphena and Tryphosa.
He remembered Persis.
Their names became part of a letter that the church continues to read centuries later.
And their example still speaks.
Not because they were perfect.
Not because we know every detail of their lives.
But because their labor in the Lord mattered.
So perhaps the next time someone asks what a successful Christian life looks like, we should be slower to point toward a platform.
Perhaps we should open Romans 16.
And remember the women who worked hard for the Gospel.
Because the church does not need more people desperate to be seen.
It needs people so captivated by Jesus that they are willing to love, serve, and remain faithful whether anyone applauds or not.
And when the world forgets your name, remember this: the Savior who died to redeem you does not need the world's applause to know you are His.
